clinicalPearls: An aggressive malignant thymic epithelial tumour that is biologically distinct from and behaves far worse than thymoma
Presents as an anterior mediastinal mass, often with chest pain, cough, breathlessness, or superior vena caval obstruction
Unlike thymoma, it is rarely associated with myasthenia gravis or other paraneoplastic autoimmune syndromes
Shows infiltrative growth with a tendency to invade adjacent structures and to metastasise to lymph nodes and distant sites
Squamous cell carcinoma is the commonest histological subtype, and loss of thymoma-associated markers helps distinguish it pathologically
Complete surgical resection when feasible offers the best chance of cure and is often combined with radiotherapy and chemotherapy
Multimodality therapy is frequently required because many tumours are locally advanced or metastatic at diagnosis
reference.pathophysiology: Thymic carcinoma arises from the epithelial cells of the thymus but, unlike thymoma, shows overtly malignant cytological features, loss of the organotypic thymic architecture, and an infiltrative, destructive growth pattern. The tumour cells lose the immature T-lymphocyte-rich background characteristic of thymoma, which underlies both the different immunohistochemical profile and the rarity of associated autoimmune syndromes. It invades local mediastinal structures including the pericardium, great vessels, and lung, and disseminates via lymphatics and the bloodstream, so a substantial proportion present with advanced or metastatic disease.
additionalInvestigations: Contrast-enhanced CT of the thorax to assess the mass and local invasion
MRI to clarify vascular or pericardial involvement
PET-CT for staging and detection of nodal and distant metastases
Core or surgical biopsy with immunohistochemistry to distinguish from thymoma and germ cell tumour
Serum germ cell tumour markers to exclude a germ cell tumour in the differential
redFlags: Superior vena caval obstruction with facial and upper limb swelling
Invasion of great vessels, pericardium, or airway on imaging
Rapidly enlarging anterior mediastinal mass with constitutional symptoms
reference.prognosis: Thymic carcinoma carries a markedly poorer prognosis than thymoma, driven by frequent local invasion and metastasis; completely resected, early-stage disease has the best outcome, while advanced disease has limited survival despite multimodality treatment.
pitfalls: Assuming an anterior mediastinal epithelial tumour is an indolent thymoma without adequate histological assessment
Expecting myasthenia gravis to be present and being falsely reassured by its absence
Understaging by omitting PET-CT and missing metastatic disease
Proceeding to incomplete resection without considering neoadjuvant therapy for locally advanced tumours
references: Murray & Nadel's Textbook of Respiratory Medicine
